JSON: Name: supernet_uncertainty_segmentation Title: SUPER-Net: training encoder-decoder segmentation networks by propagating variational mean and covariance with first-order approximations to produce simultaneous pixel-wise segmentation and uncertainty maps Short Hypothesis: Propagating the variational posterior mean and covariance through encoder-decoder layers using first-order Taylor approximations during training produces pixel-wise uncertainty estimates that correlate with segmentation errors and yield higher robustness to Gaussian noise and adversarial attacks than MC-dropout and ensemble baselines. Related Work: Semantic segmentation is dominated by encoder-decoder architectures (e.g., U-Net) and purely deterministic approaches that provide point estimates only. Uncertainty quantification approaches include MC-dropout at inference, deep ensembles, and alternate probabilistic formulations; these either (1) estimate uncertainty post hoc via repeated forward passes or multiple models, incurring substantial runtime and storage cost, or (2) provide only scalar/global uncertainty measures rather than dense pixel-wise maps. Prior variational propagation work addressed uncertainty propagation in classifiers but did not present closed-form, layer-wise derivations for up-sampling, padding, concatenation and decoder nonlinearities used in encoder-decoder segmentation, nor did they jointly learn covariance through the decoder. Existing methods are also inadequately evaluated for robustness under structured noise and targeted adversarial attacks. Abstract: We present SUPER-Net, a Bayesian training framework for encoder-decoder image segmentation that learns and propagates the first two moments of a variational posterior through all nonlinear layers to produce, per input, both a segmentation map and a dense pixel-wise uncertainty map without Monte Carlo sampling at inference. Using first-order Taylor-series approximations, SUPER-Net updates variational mean and covariance through convolution, activation, pooling, up-sampling, padding and encoder–decoder concatenation operations, enabling end-to-end ELBO optimization. The principal contribution is a set of closed-form, scalable moment-propagation rules for encoder-decoder networks together with an architecture that outputs segmentation and predictive covariance simultaneously. We evaluate SUPER-Net on chest CT, hippocampus MRI, BraTS multi-contrast MRI and a clinical FLAIR dataset under multiple Gaussian noise levels and adversarial attacks, and compare against deterministic U-Net, MC-dropout Bayes U-Net and ensemble baselines. We expect SUPER-Net to provide calibrated, spatially localized uncertainty that correlates with segmentation errors and improves robustness under distributional shifts and attacks. Experiments: Datasets: (1) Lungs CT (20 CT volumes, cropped to 512x512), (2) Hippocampus (MSD subset, 394 MRI scans, input size 64x64), (3) BraTS HGG (multimodal T1,T1c,T2,FLAIR, 240x240), (4) UAB clinical FLAIR (627 scans, 240x240). Preprocessing: normalize intensities to [0,1], remove empty slices, apply per-dataset crop/padding sizes as above. Train/val/test split: 80/10/10 stratified by patient. Baselines: deterministic U-Net, Bayes U-Net (MC-dropout with dropout=0.5 at central blocks, N=20 MC samples at inference), Ensemble U-Net (5 independently trained U-Nets). Proposed: SUPER-Net implementing variational Gaussian kernels with diagonal covariance and first-order Taylor propagation. Training: Adam lr=1e-3, batch sizes per Table 1 (or 8 for large models), 100 epochs, early stopping on val DSC. Adversarial protocols: FGSM untargeted (epsilons mapped to SNRs: {35,31,20,14,3} dB) and PGD targeted (20 iterations, step size 1, multiple source-target label pairs). Noise protocols: additive Gaussian noise applied to (a) entire image and (b) pixels within target structures, at SNRs above. Evaluation metrics: Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) per class/region, Pixel-wise predictive variance (mean and distribution), Expected Calibration Error (ECE) on segmentation confidences, ROC-AUC for detecting incorrect pixels using uncertainty as score, change in DSC after removing top-X% uncertain pixels (X=1,5,10%), inference time per image, and memory footprint. Statistical testing: report mean ± std over 5 random seeds; use paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test for DSC comparisons (p<0.05). Ablations: (A1) propagate only mean (deterministic), (A2) propagate mean + diagonal covariance vs mean + block/full covariance, (A3) encoder-only covariance propagation vs full encoder-decoder propagation, (A4) first-order Taylor approximation vs MC-based gradient estimates (N=20) during training. Additional analyses: sensitivity to prior variance (sweep 1e-6 to 1e-1), effect of kernel size and number of layers on uncertainty calibration. Report per-dataset and per-noise-level results and produce qualitative uncertainty maps for representative cases. Risk Factors and Limitations: Increased computation: forward/backward propagation of covariance doubles per-layer algebraic operations and increases inference latency relative to deterministic U-Net and may limit real-time use. Approximation error: first-order Taylor approximations may be inaccurate for highly nonlinear activations or large input perturbations, producing miscalibrated uncertainties. Covariance model: diagonal covariance assumption reduces parameters but ignores inter-kernel correlations; full covariance is computationally prohibitive. Prior sensitivity: model behavior depends on chosen Gaussian prior variance and KL weighting; poor choices can yield over/underconfident outputs. Small or imbalanced datasets: uncertainty estimates may be biased for underrepresented classes or rare structures. Adversarial adaptivity: stronger or adaptive attacks may exploit the method and reduce both accuracy and reliability of uncertainty. Generalization limits: performance measured on CT/MRI modalities may not transfer to other imaging types without re-tuning. Evaluation bias: using SNR-mapped adversarial budgets and fixed preprocessing may not reflect all clinical acquisition variability.
